title: Trump pardons former police K-9 handler Stephanie Mohr
description_medium: Trump issued a full pardon for former Prince George’s County police officer Stephanie Mohr on December 23, 2020. Mohr, the department’s first female K-9 handler, was convicted of depriving a burglary suspect of civil rights after her dog bit him; she served ten years in prison. The White House cited her service record and said the pardon restored her federal rights.
description_long:
Stephanie Mohr was a Prince George’s County police officer and the department’s first female K-9 handler. In 1995, she released her police dog on a burglary suspect, who suffered a bite wound that required ten stitches. A jury convicted Mohr of deprivation of civil rights under color of law, and the Justice Department records a 10-year prison sentence followed by two years of supervised release.

Trump granted Mohr a full pardon on December 23, 2020. The White House emphasized her law-enforcement career and support from the Law Enforcement Legal Defense Fund and Fraternal Order of Police. It described the pardon as recognition of her service and the lengthy prison term she had already served. The decision restored federal rights following her conviction. The official account frames the incident as a use-of-force case involving a police dog, while the underlying conviction treated it as a deprivation of the suspect’s civil rights.
source_access_notes: White House December 23, 2020 clemency statement read for the K-9 incident, Mohr’s department role and stated rationale; DOJ clemency table read for the conviction and sentence.
rationale: The White House describes the dog-bite incident and clemency rationale; DOJ lists Mohr’s civil-rights conviction and ten-year prison term.

title: Trump pardons former Border Patrol agent Gary Mark Brugman
description_medium: Trump granted Gary Mark Brugman a full pardon in December 2020 for a conviction arising from an encounter with people crossing near Eagle Pass, Texas. The former Border Patrol agent was convicted of deprivation of rights after being accused of knocking one man to the ground. He served 27 months in prison. The White House cited his Coast Guard and Border Patrol service.
description_long:
Gary Mark Brugman served in the Coast Guard and later as a U.S. Border Patrol agent at Eagle Pass, Texas. During an encounter with people crossing the border, Brugman and other agents pursued and apprehended nearly a dozen people. He was accused of knocking one man to the ground and was convicted of deprivation of rights under color of law. The Justice Department lists a 27-month prison term and two years of supervised release.

Trump granted Brugman a full pardon on December 23, 2020. The White House described his prior military and border-service roles, his imprisonment, and his later education and work, presenting these as reasons for clemency. The grant cleared the federal consequences of the conviction but did not change the underlying court finding. The pardon statement’s account emphasizes Brugman’s law-enforcement background, while the conviction arose from the limits federal civil-rights law places on an officer’s use of force during an apprehension.
source_access_notes: White House December 23, 2020 statement read for Brugman’s encounter, service history and stated rationale; DOJ clemency table read for offense and sentence.
rationale: The White House supplies Brugman’s account of the border encounter and support for clemency; DOJ records the civil-rights offense, 27-month prison term and supervised release.

title: Trump pardons Scott Conor Crosby for 1992 bank robbery
description_medium: Trump granted Scott Conor Crosby a full pardon on January 20, 2021, for a 1992 Arizona bank robbery committed with a co-worker. The White House said Crosby was arrested that day and cooperated with authorities. He served a little over five years in prison and later volunteered at church, mentored youth and earned EMT certification. The pardon restored his federal civil rights.
description_long:
Scott Conor Crosby was 20 when he joined a co-worker’s plan to rob a bank in Arizona in 1992. The White House described the decision as a spur-of-the-moment mistake, said Crosby was arrested the same day, and noted that he cooperated with authorities. The Justice Department records convictions for bank robbery and using a firearm during a crime of violence, with a sentence of 60 months and two days in prison followed by three years of supervised release.

Trump issued Crosby a full pardon on January 20, 2021. The White House listed support from Senator Martha McSally, Mesa’s mayor and vice mayor, and Crosby’s church bishop. It also said Arizona had restored his state civil rights in 2003 and that the federal pardon restored his federal rights. After prison, Crosby volunteered through his church, mentored young people, and earned an emergency medical technician certification. The clemency statement framed the grant around his cooperation, community support, and rehabilitation after the robbery conviction.
source_access_notes: White House January 20, 2021 statement read for the robbery account, supporters, and restoration of rights; DOJ clemency table read for Crosby’s offenses and sentence.
rationale: The White House details Crosby’s role in the robbery, cooperation and post-release work; DOJ confirms the robbery and firearm convictions and prison term.

title: Trump pardons coal-industry manager Thomas Kenton “Ken” Ford
description_medium: Trump granted a full pardon to coal-industry manager Thomas Kenton “Ken” Ford in January 2021. Ford pleaded guilty after making a material misstatement to federal mining officials and served three years’ probation. The White House said his supporters in the mining sector praised his safety work and professionalism. DOJ lists his conviction under the name Thomas K. Ford; its index gives January 13, while the White House announcement came January 20.
description_long:
Thomas Kenton “Ken” Ford worked for decades in the coal industry and was a general manager at a coal company when Trump pardoned him. The Justice Department’s clemency list records a Southern District of Illinois conviction for violating mandatory safety standards and making false material statements or representations; Ford received three years’ probation and a $2,000 fine. The White House said Ford had pleaded guilty after making a material misstatement to federal mining officials about twenty years earlier.

The White House announced the pardon on January 20, 2021, and described support from people in mining operations, safety, and engineering who praised Ford’s professionalism and work to keep miners safe. The Justice Department index groups the case under January 13, 2021, so the public record distinguishes its listed date from the announcement date. The administration’s rationale focused on Ford’s later career and his use of experience from the case to promote safety and truthful dealings with federal mining officials.
source_access_notes: White House January 20, 2021 statement read for Ford’s coal-sector role, offense summary and supporters; DOJ clemency table read for the formal case name, offenses, sentence and January 13 listing date.
rationale: The White House identifies Ford as Ken Ford and explains his mining work and pardon support; DOJ identifies Thomas K. Ford’s conviction and lists the case under January 13, while the announcement is dated January 20.

title: Trump pardons New Jersey surgeon Frederick Nahas for obstructing Medicare investigation
description_medium: Trump granted surgeon Frederick J. Nahas a full pardon in January 2021. Nahas pleaded guilty to obstructing the communication of records in a federal investigation into his Medicare billing practices and served one month in prison. The White House said investigators found no underlying billing fraud and cited his later work to rebuild trust with patients and colleagues; DOJ lists an additional fine and supervised release.
description_long:
Frederick J. Nahas was a New Jersey surgeon whose Medicare billing practices became the subject of a federal investigation in the 1990s. He pleaded guilty in 2002 to preventing, obstructing, misleading, or delaying the communication of information and records about a health-care investigation. A federal administrative decision records a one-month prison term followed by home confinement and weekend placement at a community corrections facility; the Justice Department’s clemency table also lists supervised release and a $20,000 fine.

Trump granted Nahas a full pardon in January 2021. The White House said the six-year investigation uncovered no underlying billing fraud, but that Nahas had not fully cooperated; it cited his later effort to regain the trust of patients, colleagues, and the community. It also named Representative Jeff Van Drew as a supporter. The pardon addressed the obstruction conviction, not a finding that the underlying billing investigation had established fraud. DOJ lists the grant under January 13, while the White House’s clemency announcement was issued January 20.
source_access_notes: White House January 20 statement read for the stated pardon basis and its account of the investigation; HHS administrative decision read for Nahas’s guilty plea and confinement terms; DOJ clemency table read for the listed offenses, fine, and January 13 date heading.
rationale: HHS records the obstruction plea and sentence; the White House states that the billing investigation found no underlying fraud and describes the later pardon rationale. DOJ groups the grant under January 13, while the public announcement followed on January 20.
